title: Zigzag Star Pattern
description: Brute force to optimized: a per-column closed-form reflection formula versus a running bounce pointer, then a further space-optimized version that builds each row directly with no auxiliary array.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given a positive integer n, the number of columns, print a zigzag wave of stars across a fixed 4 rows and n columns: the star position starts at row 0, moves down one row per column until it reaches row 3, then moves back up one row per column until it reaches row 0, repeating this bounce for as many columns as needed.

blocks.text: Given a positive integer n, print a zigzag wave of stars across a fixed 4 rows and n columns: the star position starts at row 0, moves down one row per column until it reaches row 3, then moves back up one row per column until it reaches row 0, repeating this bounce for as many columns as the input requires.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Ball Bouncing Between a Floor and a Ceiling
blocks.text: Picture a ball dropped between a floor and a ceiling four rows apart. Each column is one moment in time: the ball moves down one row, and the instant it touches the ceiling or the floor, it reverses direction and moves back the other way, tracing the same zigzag shape forever.

blocks.caption: The star position bounces between row 0 and row 3, one row per column

blocks.content: {"headers":["Row","Output","Why"],"rows":[["Row 0","*     *  ","The bounce touches row 0 at columns 0 and 6, the two moments the ball is at the top"],["Row 1"," *   * * ","Row 1 is crossed on the way down (column 1) and on the way up, twice more (columns 5 and 7)"],["Row 2","  * *   *","Row 2 is crossed on the way down (column 2), on the way up (column 4), and again starting the next descent (column 8)"],["Row 3","   *     ","The bounce only reaches the very bottom once in 9 columns, at column 3, before heading back up"]]}

blocks.text: With only 4 columns, the ball has just enough room to travel from the ceiling to the floor once, without yet bouncing back: *    /  *   /   *  /    *.
A single column only ever shows the very first moment of the bounce, the star at row 0, with the remaining three rows blank.
Before writing any code, notice that the star's row position changes by exactly one row between any two neighboring columns, it is never computed independently from scratch.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The row sequence across columns is 0, 1, 2, 3, 2, 1, 0, 1, 2, 3, ... a value that changes by exactly plus 1 or minus 1 at every step, never jumping.

Observation 2: The direction only ever needs to flip at the two boundary rows, row 0 and row 3, exactly where a bouncing ball would hit the ceiling or the floor.

Observation 3: This sequence has period 6 (down 0 to 3 takes 3 steps, up 3 to 0 takes 3 more), so the row at column c can also be reached by reflecting c mod 6 back into the 0 to 3 range.

Observation 4: Tracking a running row and a running direction avoids the reflection arithmetic entirely, and generalizes immediately if the row count ever changed.
Two equally valid approaches follow from this: compute each column's row directly with a closed-form reflection formula, or simulate the bounce with a running pointer and a direction flag.
For every column, compute its star row directly from the closed-form reflection of c mod 6 back into the 0 to 3 range, store the full 4 by n grid, then print it.

items: For every column c from 0 to n minus 1, compute m = c mod 6.
Reflect m back into the 0 to 3 range: if m is greater than 3, the row is 6 minus m, otherwise the row is m itself.
Mark that (row, c) position with a star in a full 4 by n grid of spaces.
Print all 4 rows of the grid, top to bottom.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: reflect c mod 6 into a row, for every single column independently

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: A full 4 by n grid of spaces is allocated up front, so every position starts blank and only the star positions need to be overwritten.
The reflection formula, m if m is at most 3 otherwise 6 minus m, is recomputed independently for every single column, with no memory of the previous column's row.
Printing happens only after the entire grid has been filled, one pass over every row.

blocks.text: Every column lands on the correct row, since the reflection formula is applied directly to its own position.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(rows times n), a constant 4 times n, since every one of the n columns needs one reflection computation and one grid write.
Space: O(rows times n) for the full grid, even though only one cell per column is ever a star.

Limitation: the grid stores far more than is ever needed, 4 times n cells when only n of them are stars, and the reflection formula must be re-derived correctly for every column instead of reusing the previous column's answer.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why compute the row from scratch every time: the reflection formula works, but it treats every column as an independent problem, ignoring that neighboring columns differ by exactly one row.

What is the actual relationship between neighboring columns: the row moves by plus 1 or minus 1 from one column to the next, never further.

When does the direction change: only at the two boundary rows, row 0 and row 3, exactly where the bounce reverses.

Can the full 2D grid be avoided: yes, only one star row per column ever matters, so a single array of n values (or even no array at all) replaces the full 4 by n grid.

The core idea: track a running row and a running direction, flipping the direction only at the two boundary rows, instead of re-deriving every column's row independently.

Track a current row and a direction, starting at row 0 moving downward. After recording each column's row, flip the direction whenever the current row is about to move past row 0 or row 3, and store the answer in a single array of length n instead of a full 4 by n grid.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: track one running row and direction, flipping only at the two boundary rows

blocks.text: Recording the running row for every column is exactly equivalent to the closed-form reflection, since both describe the same bounce, but tracking it directly needs only a comparison and an addition per column instead of a modulo and a reflection formula, and it generalizes immediately if the number of rows ever changed.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(rows times n), the same order as the brute force, but with simpler, cheaper per-column work.
Space: O(n) for the star row array, down from O(rows times n) for the full grid.
10. Further Optimization: Building Each Row Directly, No Array

The running-pointer version above already drops the space from a full grid down to one array of length n, but that array still stores information for every column even though each row only touches roughly a quarter of them. Since the bounce has period 6 (3 steps down, 3 steps up), each of the 4 fixed rows can be built directly by striding through its own matching columns, with no auxiliary array of any size.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Offsets within one period of 6","Matching columns for row 2","Why"],"rows":[["2 and 4","2, 4, 8, 10","Row 2 is touched once on the way down (offset 2) and once on the way up (offset 4) in every period of 6 columns"]]}

blocks.caption: Further optimization: derive each row's star columns directly from the period, no array at all

items: period is 2 times (rows minus 1), the number of columns it takes to go from row 0 down to the last row and back, 6 for 4 rows.
The descending pass marks every column at offset row, row + period, row + 2 times period, and so on.
Interior rows (not the two boundary rows) also get an ascending pass, at offset period minus row, since those rows are crossed twice per period.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(rows times n), unchanged, every star position still needs to be written once.
Space: O(1) extra beyond the single row string being built, no auxiliary array covering all n columns is ever kept.

blocks.text: The zigzag pattern looks like a geometry problem, but its real structure is a bouncing sequence with a fixed period, once that period is recognized, the whole pattern can be built either by simulating the bounce column by column, or by striding directly through each row's matching columns without any array at all.

items: Forgetting to flip the direction at both boundary rows, only handling the bottom and not the top (or vice versa).
Allocating a full rows by n grid when only one star position per column is ever needed.
Getting the ascending-pass offset wrong for interior rows, it is period minus row, not row itself.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["n = 0","Produces no output at all."],["n = 1","A single star at row 0, the other 3 rows entirely blank."]]}

blocks.text: Describing the row position as a value that bounces between two boundaries, exactly like a ball between a floor and a ceiling, is usually the fastest way to make the direction-flip logic obvious, and mentioning the fixed period, 2 times rows minus 1, shows the pattern has been fully understood rather than just simulated.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you avoid the full 2D grid", think: track only the current row and direction, one array of size n instead of rows times n.
If the interviewer says "can you avoid extra space entirely", think: build each fixed row directly by striding through its matching columns using the period.
If the interviewer says "what if the number of rows changed", think: the running-pointer version generalizes immediately, only the boundary check changes.

items: How would the direction-flip logic change if the pattern used 6 rows instead of 4?
Can you derive the closed-form reflection formula directly from the running-pointer simulation?
How would you build the pattern column by column instead of row by row, printing top to bottom as columns arrive one at a time?
What is the period in terms of the row count, and why is it exactly twice the number of interior bounces?
Any pattern-printing problem where a position moves by a fixed step and reflects off a boundary, the same running-pointer technique applies directly.
The reflection formula here is the same idea used to fold a value back into a fixed range, seen again in problems that map a growing index onto a small cyclic range.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force and optimized versions both run in O(rows times n) time; space drops from O(rows times n) for the full grid, to O(n) for the running-pointer array, to O(1) extra for the direct per-row stride version.

items: Pattern: a bouncing-pointer pattern, the star position moves by one row per column and reflects off two fixed boundary rows.
Core Idea: track a running row and direction, flipping direction only at the two boundary rows, instead of computing each column's row independently.
Time: O(rows times n) for all three approaches.
Space: O(rows times n) for the brute force grid, O(n) for the running-pointer array, O(1) extra for the direct per-row stride version.
Most Important Observation: the star row changes by exactly one between neighboring columns, so it never needs to be recomputed from scratch.
Interview Difficulty: straightforward once the bounce is recognized; the direction-flip boundary condition is the one detail worth double-checking.
One line memory trick: a ball bouncing between a floor and a ceiling, one row per column.
